alt: Four numbered stages in a row: aims and hypotheses, pilot study, sampling, analysis of data. Below, an aim is a general statement such as investigating how couples divide housework, while a hypothesis is a narrower, testable prediction such as dual-career couples sharing housework more equally.
caption: Plan the aim, test the method, choose the sample, then analyse.

alt: Four panels. Random: scattered people chosen, each with an equal chance. Systematic: every nth name on a list. Quota: set numbers filled for each group, such as 78 women and 72 men in a sample of 150 from a town that is 52% female. Snowball: one participant introduces the next in a chain. Each has a strength and a weakness.
caption: Each sampling method trades fairness, speed and reach against representativeness.

alt: A line runs from quantitative methods, which are more reliable and easy to compare, to qualitative methods, which give more depth and validity. Questionnaires, structured interviews, unstructured interviews and participant observation are placed along it with a strength and a weakness each. Below, mixed methods combine both.
caption: Quantitative methods favour reliability; qualitative methods favour validity; mixed methods combine them.

alt: A two-by-two grid. Columns: participant observation, where the researcher joins the group, and non-participant, where they only watch. Rows: overt, where the group knows, and covert, where it is secret. Overt observation may change behaviour; covert observation breaks informed consent.
caption: Joining or watching, openly or in secret: each choice trades validity against ethics.

alt: A two-by-two grid. Primary quantitative: your own closed questionnaire or structured interviews. Primary qualitative: your own unstructured interviews or observations. Secondary quantitative: official and non-official statistics. Secondary qualitative: diaries, letters, media content, websites and earlier studies. Below, primary data fit the aim but cost more; secondary data are cheap but made for another purpose.
caption: Any source can be sorted two ways: who collected it, and whether it is numbers or words.

alt: Three bars for the same society in 1968–69: just over 6% in poverty on the state standard, a little over 9% on relative income, and more than 22% on Townsend’s relative deprivation measure.
caption: The same society can show 6%, 9% or 22% in poverty, depending on the definition.

alt: Two bars for a fictional town: 28% of couples said they shared housework equally in 2005 and 42% in 2025. The rise is 14 percentage points, which is a 50% increase on the starting figure. Saying it rose by 14% would be wrong.
caption: A rise from 28% to 42% is 14 percentage points, or a 50% increase.

alt: Three cards: consent, addressed by explaining aims, written and parental consent and the right to withdraw; confidentiality, addressed by anonymising and storing data securely; harm, addressed by avoiding distressing questions, allowing people to stop and debriefing. Below, the case for and against covert observation.
caption: Consent, confidentiality and harm each have practical fixes; covert observation tests them all.
